title: Chapter 28 — Ahab
paragraphs: For several days after leaving Nantucket, Captain Ahab was nowhere to be seen above decks. The mates relieved each other at their watches as usual, and to all appearances they seemed to be the only commanders of the ship. But sometimes they emerged from the cabin with orders so sudden and absolute that it was clear they were only commanding on someone else's authority. Yes, their supreme lord and ruler was down there, though still unseen by any eyes not permitted to enter the now sacred retreat of the cabin.

Every time I came up on deck from my watches below, I instantly looked aft for any strange face. My first vague unease about the unknown captain, now intensified by the isolation of the open sea, had become a real anxiety. This was strangely heightened at times by ragged Elijah's wild, incoherent warnings, which kept coming back to me uninvited, with a disturbing power I hadn't imagined possible. I couldn't resist them, even though in calmer moments I was almost ready to laugh at the solemn absurdities of that odd prophet of the wharves. But whatever my apprehension — if I can call it that — whenever I looked around the ship, it seemed completely unjustified. The harpooners and the bulk of the crew were a far more wild, heathen, and mixed lot than any merchant ship company I had known. But I attributed this, rightly, to the fierce uniqueness of the wild Scandinavian trade I had so recklessly joined. What truly calmed my nameless fears and inspired confidence about the voyage was the character of the three chief officers — the mates. Three better, more capable sea-officers and men, each in his own different way, could not easily be found, and every one of them was American — a Nantucketer, a Vineyarder, and a Cape man. Now, since the ship had left harbor on Christmas Day, we had biting polar weather for a while, though always running south away from it. With every degree of latitude we sailed, we gradually left that merciless winter behind. It was one of those less threatening but still gray and gloomy transitional mornings, when the ship was rushing through the water with a vengeful sort of leaping, melancholy speed, that I came up on deck at the call of the forenoon watch. The moment I leveled my gaze toward the stern, a shiver of foreboding ran through me. Reality outran my worst fears: Captain Ahab stood upon his quarter-deck.

There was no sign of ordinary illness about him, nor of recovery from any. He looked like a man cut down from the burning stake, when the fire has consumed all his limbs' outer surface without destroying them or diminishing their compact, aged strength. His entire tall, broad frame seemed made of solid bronze, cast in an unchangeable mold, like Cellini's statue of Perseus. Threading its way out from among his gray hairs and continuing down one side of his tawny, scorched face and neck until it disappeared into his clothing, you could see a slender, rod-like mark, lividly white. It resembled the vertical seam sometimes left in the straight, tall trunk of a great tree when lightning tears down it, peeling and grooving the bark from top to bottom without breaking a single branch, then running off into the ground, leaving the tree still greenly alive but branded. Whether that mark was something he was born with, or the scar of some desperate wound, no one could say for sure. By unspoken agreement, throughout the voyage little or no mention was made of it, especially by the mates. But once an old Gay Head Indian among the crew, Tashtego's elder, superstitiously claimed that Ahab didn't get that mark until he was a full forty years old, and that it came upon him not in any human fight but in an elemental struggle at sea. Yet this wild theory seemed to be contradicted by what a gray old Manxman suggested — an ancient, grave man who, having never before sailed out of Nantucket, had never seen wild Ahab before. Nevertheless, old sea traditions and ancient superstitions credited this Manxman with supernatural powers of perception. So no white sailor seriously argued when he said that if Captain Ahab should ever be peacefully laid out — which might hardly come to pass, he muttered — then whoever performed that last service for the dead would find a birthmark on him running from crown to sole.

So powerfully did Ahab's entire grim appearance affect me, and the livid brand that streaked his face, that for the first few moments I hardly noticed that much of this overpowering grimness was due to the barbaric white leg on which he partly stood. I had heard that this ivory leg had been fashioned at sea from the polished bone of a sperm whale's jaw. "Yes, he lost his mast off Japan," the old Gay Head Indian once said, "but like his dismasted ship, he fitted another mast without going home for it. He has a whole supply of them."

I was struck by the singular posture he maintained. On each side of the Pequod's quarter-deck, close to the mizzen shrouds, an auger hole had been bored about half an inch into the plank. His bone leg was steadied in that hole. One arm raised, holding onto a shroud, Captain Ahab stood erect, staring straight out beyond the ship's ever-pitching bow. There was an infinity of iron determination in that gaze — a fixed, fearless, forward dedication that would not surrender. He spoke not a word, nor did his officers say anything to him. Yet by their every small gesture and expression, they clearly showed their uneasy, even painful awareness of being under a troubled master's eye. And more than that — moody, stricken Ahab stood before them with a crucifixion in his face, with all the nameless, regal, overpowering dignity of some mighty grief.

Before long, after his first appearance on deck, he withdrew to his cabin. But after that morning, he was visible to the crew every day — either standing in his pivot-hole, or sitting on an ivory stool he had, or walking heavily across the deck. As the sky grew less gloomy and even began to turn mild, he became less and less of a recluse, as if, when the ship first sailed from home, nothing but the dead winter bleakness of the sea had kept him shut away. Gradually, he was almost constantly in the open air. But for all he said or visibly did on the now sunny deck, he seemed as unnecessary there as an extra mast. The Pequod was only making a passage, not actively cruising. Nearly all the whaling preparations that needed overseeing the mates were fully capable of handling. So there was little outside of himself to occupy or excite Ahab, and nothing to chase away the clouds that piled, layer upon layer, upon his brow — just as storm clouds always choose the tallest peaks to gather on.

Nevertheless, before long, the warm, coaxing charm of the pleasant, holiday weather we sailed into seemed to gradually draw him from his dark mood. For just as when the rosy, dancing girls of April and May come tripping home to the wintry, bitter woods, even the barest, roughest, most thunder-split old oak will at least send out a few green sprouts to welcome such cheerful visitors — so Ahab did, in the end, respond a little to the playful temptations of that gentle air. More than once, he put forth the faint blossom of a look which, in any other man, would soon have flowered into a smile.
